summary: Specifies IPv4 compatibility mechanisms for IPv6 hosts and routers: dual stack and configured tunneling. Dual stack means implementing both IP versions, and configured tunneling carries IPv6 packets across IPv4 networks. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4213 describes two ways for IPv6 hosts and routers to remain compatible with IPv4. A node can implement both versions of IP, or it can carry IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets between configured endpoints.

questions: how does ipv6 over ipv4 tunneling work
what is the ipv6 tunnel mtu
subtitle: Dual-stack operation and configured tunnels for IPv6 nodes that must work with IPv4.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts and routers need to interoperate while IPv4 infrastructure and IPv4-only nodes remain in use.
tldr.mechanism: Dual-stack nodes implement both IP versions. Configured tunnels encapsulate IPv6 packets in IPv4 and carry them between explicitly configured endpoints.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines basic compatibility behavior, including tunnel MTU rules and source-address checks. It obsoletes RFC 2893.

today: RFC 4213 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It obsoletes RFC 2893; the unit metadata lists no later update.

sections.title: Two Basic Transition Mechanisms
sections.content:
IPv6 deployment must work alongside the installed base of IPv4 hosts and routers. RFC 4213 defines two mechanisms for IPv6/IPv4 nodes: a dual IP layer and configured IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling.

These mechanisms form part of a transition toolbox. Sites and implementations choose which tools fit their needs; other transition methods are outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 nodes need to communicate while much of the network still uses IPv4. This RFC describes dual-stack operation and configured tunnels as two ways to do that.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Hosts and Routers
sections.content:
A dual-stack node has complete IPv4 and IPv6 implementations. It can communicate with an IPv4 node using IPv4 and with an IPv6 node using IPv6. Either stack may be enabled or disabled for operational reasons.

Dual-stack nodes acquire IPv4 and IPv6 addresses using mechanisms for each protocol. Their resolver libraries must handle both IPv4 A records and IPv6 AAAA records; when an application requests both, the resolver must not filter either family out.
sections.plainLanguage: A dual-stack node can send and receive both IPv4 and IPv6 packets. Its name resolver must be able to return addresses for either version.

sections.title: Encapsulating IPv6 in IPv4
sections.content:
A configured tunnel has an encapsulator and a decapsulator. The encapsulator places an IPv4 header before the IPv6 packet; the decapsulator reassembles the IPv4 packet if needed, removes that header, and passes the IPv6 packet to its IPv6 layer.

The outer IPv4 header uses protocol number 41. Its source address identifies the encapsulator and its destination identifies the tunnel endpoint. The endpoints are configured, and the tunnel is treated as a bidirectional point-to-point link.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel entrance puts an IPv4 header around an IPv6 packet, and the exit removes it. IPv4 routers can then carry the packet without processing its IPv6 contents.

sections.title: Tunnel MTU and Fragmentation
sections.content:
An encapsulator must not treat a tunnel as having an MTU near 64 kilobytes. The RFC defines a static tunnel MTU and an optional dynamic MTU based on IPv4 Path MTU Discovery.

The default static MTU must be from 1280 through 1480 bytes and should be 1280 bytes. Dynamic MTU uses the IPv4 path MTU minus the 20-byte IPv4 header; if that result is below 1280 bytes, the encapsulator may need to fragment the IPv4 packet. Dropped ICMPv4 messages can cause path-MTU black holes.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel must use a realistic packet-size limit rather than assume every packet fits. It can use a fixed size or measure the IPv4 path, but blocked error messages can prevent the measurement from working.

sections.title: Forwarding and Decapsulation Rules
sections.content:
IPv6 treats the tunnel as a single hop, so the IPv6 hop limit is reduced when forwarding into or out of it. The decapsulator must check that the outer IPv4 source address matches the configured tunnel endpoint before accepting a packet.

The decapsulator must support IPv6 packets and IPv4 reassembly of at least 1500 bytes, subject to the larger interface MTU described by the RFC. It must discard invalid IPv6 source addresses. Configured tunnels also need link-local addresses and must process Neighbor Unreachability Detection probes.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving endpoint checks that a tunneled packet came from the configured peer before passing it to IPv6. It also applies IPv6 source-address and neighbor-discovery rules.

sections.title: Preventing Spoofed Tunnel Traffic
sections.content:
A tunnel can span an untrusted network. Without checks, an attacker could send an IPv4 packet to the decapsulator containing a forged IPv6 source address and bypass ordinary ingress filtering.

The decapsulator must verify the configured IPv4 tunnel source and discard obviously invalid IPv6 sources. IPv6 ingress filtering should also be used. If stronger protection is needed, the RFC recommends an authenticated tunnel such as IPsec; it also describes GRE with a preconfigured key.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel must not let an outside sender inject packets with a forged inner source address. Checking the configured tunnel endpoint helps, and IPsec can add authentication and integrity protection.
